subtype: Approach: caring for own limits and feelings [Revision]
passage: Come sit, beta. Your Aditi Masi has a story. When I was sixteen, my friend Sonali went through a very dark stretch, and I was the one she called, sometimes three times a night. I never said no. Then one morning I was crying into my cereal for no reason, and my hands wouldn't stop trembling before a test. I realised I had nothing left. That evening I told Amma all of it. She didn't scold me. She hugged me, and the next day we phoned Sonali's mother together and spoke to the school counsellor. I stayed her friend, sat beside her at lunch and slipped silly notes into her bag. But I stopped being her only rope. That was the kindest thing I did, for both of us.

qa.q: Who did Aditi tell that evening?
qa.a: Aditi told Amma that evening, all of it.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling before she spoke to Amma?
qa.a: Aditi was exhausted and anxious: she cried into her cereal for no reason, her hands trembled before a test and she had nothing left.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling Amma was the turning point, because it brought in Sonali's mother and the counsellor, so Aditi could stay a friend without being Sonali's only support.

qa.q: How might Sonali have experienced Aditi sharing the support with adults?
qa.a: Sonali may have felt worried or exposed at first, yet she gained more people who could help, while Aditi still sat beside her at lunch and slipped notes into her bag.

grounding: After heavy conversations a teen notices her exhaustion and anxiety, tells her mother, shares the support with adults and keeps a friendly role.
